text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- A new record number of 201,330 early retirements was recorded in February.
- Papermaker KNP Leykam will start a joint venture with Singapore's paper expert APRIL in China to produce wood-free products.
- Insurance holding BARC, consisting of insurers Bundeslaender and Austria Collegialitaet, plans to present joint products of the two insurers from 1998 onwards.
- Austria's ailing tourism industry sees hopes rising again as researchers expect a slight upturn in the summer even though Austrians plan to save money on their holidays.
- Bureaucracy and high telephone and labour costs are the main negative aspects of working in Austria, a study among U.S. companies based in the country shows.
- Points maker VAE plans to further expand business in eastern Europe as subsidiaries abroad are raising turnover. The company's dividend will remain unchanged at 32 schillings.
- State-owned holding OeIAG has been praised by the audit office for its role in the government's privatisations.
- Rumours are spreading in Paris and Brussels that former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky is to play a major role in the European Union's Common Foreign and Security Policy.

- United Telekom Austria, a joint-venture of Austria's provincial energy providers, plans to build the country's first private telephone network as well as possibly bid for the third mobile phone licence. Plans to join forces with tele.ring, the federal railway's and federal grid Verbund's telecommunications company, are progressing at a slow pace.
- Operating costs for houses and flats are on the rise while rents are remaining stable.
- Opposition parties do not believe the government's assertion that no further austerity measures would be necessary in order to meet the Maastricht criteria.
- The conservative People's Party wants net payments of EU members to be subtracted from the respective country's deficit.
- Federal railways company OeBB plans to start a "virtual" liberalisation this year ahead of the real thing planned for 1998.
- The postal system wants communities to pay for the 200 million schilling deficit of the regional Post Bus network.
